# Settings

Analysis choices in one place. Everything else (sample end, break dates,
number of clusters) is computed from the data.

```{r settings}
SAMPLE_START    <- as.Date("1986-01-01")  # start of the modeling sample
MAX_GAP_FILL    <- 1                      # fill internal gaps up to this many months
BP_MAX_BREAKS   <- 5                      # most structural breaks the test considers (RQ1)
BP_N_BREAKS     <- 3                      # breaks used (RQ1); BIC picks the max here, see C4
K_RANGE         <- 2:8                    # cluster counts shown in diagnostics (RQ2)
K_CLUSTERS      <- 3                      # clusters used (RQ2); silhouette is flat, see C5
LABEL_WINDOW_DAYS <- 2                    # days after a decision to read the new target (RQ3)
RQ3_START_TRAIN <- 200                    # meetings in the first training window
RQ3_STEP        <- 12                     # meetings per test block
RQ3_SEED        <- 597                    # seed for the bootstrap (RQ3)
RQ3_BOOT_REPS   <- 1000                   # bootstrap resamples for score intervals (RQ3)
RQ3_BOOT_BLOCK  <- 8                      # meetings per bootstrap block (~1 year)

# Events tested with Chow tests alongside the estimated break dates (RQ1)
CHOW_EVENT_DATES <- as.Date(c(
  "2001-09-01",  # 9/11
  "2008-01-01",  # start of 2008 easing
  "2008-11-01",  # zero lower bound reached
  "2020-03-01"   # COVID
))
```

# Load Data

```{r}
set.seed(597)
# Produced by R/acquire_data.R
df_raw <- read.csv("data/macro_monthly.csv")

dim(df_raw)
colnames(df_raw)
head(df_raw)
```

# Initial Data Checks

```{r}
# missing values by column
colSums(is.na(df_raw))

# duplicated rows
sum(duplicated(df_raw))

# blank strings in character columns
sapply(df_raw[, sapply(df_raw, is.character), drop = FALSE], function(x) sum(trimws(x) == ""))

# check whether date conversion may fail
if ("date" %in% names(df_raw)) {
  sum(is.na(as.Date(df_raw$date)))
  range(as.Date(df_raw$date), na.rm = TRUE)
}

# look for columns with only one unique value
sapply(df_raw, function(x) length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])))

# check for infinite values in numeric columns
sapply(df_raw[, sapply(df_raw, is.numeric), drop = FALSE], function(x) sum(is.infinite(x)))

# inspect suspicious numeric ranges
summary(df_raw[, sapply(df_raw, is.numeric), drop = FALSE])
```

```{r}
raw_dates  <- as.Date(df_raw$date)
na_share   <- sort(colMeans(is.na(df_raw[, -1])), decreasing = TRUE)
most_missing <- names(na_share[na_share > 0.2])
```

The raw dataset has `r sum(duplicated(df_raw))` duplicate rows and covers `r format(min(raw_dates))` to `r format(max(raw_dates))`. The main issue is missingness: series that start later (`r paste(most_missing, collapse = ", ")`) are missing for more than 20% of months, and the most recent months are incomplete because of publication delays. These are handled in the cleaning steps below.

# Data Cleaning

## Fix Variable Types

```{r}
df_clean <- df_raw %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))
```

The date variable was converted to `Date` format so the dataset could be filtered, joined, and ordered consistently in later preprocessing steps.

## Remove Invalid or Incomplete Observations

```{r}
# Sample end: the last month in which every series has been published.
# Series are released with different delays, so later months are incomplete.
series_cols <- setdiff(names(df_clean), "date")

last_obs <- sapply(series_cols, function(col) {
  max(df_clean$date[!is.na(df_clean[[col]])])
})
SAMPLE_END <- as.Date(min(last_obs))

sort(as.Date(last_obs))  # last available month per series

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  filter(date <= SAMPLE_END)
```

The sample ends in `r format(SAMPLE_END, "%B %Y")`, the last month in which every series has been published. Later months are dropped because some series are released with a delay of one to two months.

## Handle Missing Values

```{r}
# Fill short gaps inside a series (e.g. October 2025, when the government
# shutdown stopped some releases) by carrying the last value forward.
# Carrying forward never uses later data, so it adds no look-ahead.
# Leading NAs (before a series starts) are left alone.
before <- df_clean

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(across(
    all_of(series_cols),
    ~ zoo::na.locf(.x, na.rm = FALSE, maxgap = MAX_GAP_FILL)
  ))

filled <- map_dfr(series_cols, function(col) {
  idx <- which(is.na(before[[col]]) & !is.na(df_clean[[col]]))
  tibble(series = col, date = before$date[idx], filled_with = df_clean[[col]][idx])
})
filled
```

`r nrow(filled)` value(s) were missing inside a series and filled with the previous month's value: `r paste(filled$series, format(filled$date, "%b %Y"), collapse = ", ")`.

Oil prices come from `WTISPLC`, the monthly WTI spot price, which has a longer history than the daily series.

# Feature Engineering

## Create Derived Variables

```{r}
df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    core_pce_yoy      = 100 * (PCEPILFE / lag(PCEPILFE, 12) - 1),
    unrate_lag1       = lag(UNRATE, 1),
    payems_yoy        = 100 * (PAYEMS / lag(PAYEMS, 12) - 1),
    term_spread_10y_3m = DGS10 - DGS3MO,
    inflation_gap     = core_pce_yoy - 2
  )
```

Several derived variables were created to better capture macroeconomic conditions relevant to policy decisions, including core inflation growth, lagged unemployment, payroll growth, the term spread, and the inflation gap relative to the 2 percent target.

## Create Target-Related Variables

```{r}
# Produced by R/acquire_data.R. Keep meetings and conference calls; drop
# notation votes and the cancelled March 2020 meeting. `date` is the first day
# of the meeting, as in the original fed_meetings.csv.
fomc_meetings <- read.csv("data/fomc_meetings.csv") %>%
  filter(!type %in% c("cancelled", "notation_vote")) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(start_date))

fomc_monthly <- fomc_meetings %>%
  mutate(month = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01"))) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    fomc_meetings    = n(),
    fomc_scheduled   = sum(is_scheduled, na.rm = TRUE),
    fomc_unscheduled = sum(!is_scheduled, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  mutate(month = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01"))) %>%
  left_join(fomc_monthly, by = "month") %>%
  mutate(
    fomc_meetings    = dplyr::coalesce(fomc_meetings, 0),
    fomc_scheduled   = dplyr::coalesce(fomc_scheduled, 0),
    fomc_unscheduled = dplyr::coalesce(fomc_unscheduled, 0)
  )
```

Monthly FOMC meeting counts were merged into the main dataset so the analysis could distinguish between months with scheduled meetings, unscheduled meetings, and no meetings.

```{r}
fomc_dates <- fomc_meetings %>%
  arrange(date)

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    days_since_last_fomc = as.numeric(date - max(fomc_dates$date[fomc_dates$date < date]))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-month)
```

The variable `days_since_last_fomc` was added to measure how much time had passed since the most recent FOMC meeting, providing a simple timing feature related to policy activity.

```{r}
df_final <- df_clean %>%
  filter(date >= SAMPLE_START)
```

After preprocessing and feature construction, the final working dataset was restricted to the post-1986 period to align with the availability of the selected variables and the scope of the modeling analysis.

# Final Modeling Dataset

The final modeling dataset is obtained after preprocessing, variable replacement, and feature engineering. The sample is restricted to the post-1986 period so that the analysis is based on a more consistent set of available variables. This dataset is used as the input for the remaining exploratory and modeling steps.

```{r}
dim(df_final)
head(df_final)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Distribution Checks

```{r}
ggplot(df_final, aes(x = ff_target)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Federal Funds Target Rate",
    x = "Federal Funds Target Rate",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(df_final, aes(x = date, y = ff_target)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Federal Funds Target Rate Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Federal Funds Target Rate"
  )
```

```{r}
missing_summary <- colSums(is.na(df_final))

missing_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(missing_summary),
  Missing_Count = as.numeric(missing_summary)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing_Count))

missing_df %>%
  filter(Missing_Count > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Variable, Missing_Count), y = Missing_Count)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Missing Values by Variable",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Number of Missing Values"
  )
```

The distribution of the federal funds target rate and its movement over time were examined to understand the scale and temporal behavior of the response variable. Missing-value patterns were also reviewed to identify whether any variables still contained gaps after preprocessing.

## Relationship Exploration

```{r}
candidate_vars <- c("UNRATE", "PCEPI", "DGS10", "T10Y3M")
selected_vars <- candidate_vars[candidate_vars %in% names(df_final)]

if (length(selected_vars) > 0) {
  df_long <- df_final %>%
    select(date, all_of(selected_vars)) %>%
    pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value")

  ggplot(df_long, aes(x = date, y = Value)) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Selected Predictors Over Time",
      x = "Date",
      y = "Value"
    )
}
```

```{r}
numeric_df <- df_final %>% select(where(is.numeric))

cor_mat <- cor(numeric_df, use = "complete.obs")

cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", midpoint = 0) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Heatmap of Numeric Variables",
    x = "",
    y = "",
    fill = "Correlation"
  )
```

Selected macroeconomic predictors were examined over time to compare their movement with changes in the policy target. Correlation analysis was also used to identify strong linear relationships among numeric variables, which is useful for understanding redundancy and potential multicollinearity in later modeling steps.

## Key EDA Findings

Overall, the exploratory analysis showed that the dataset is time-ordered and contains variables that vary meaningfully across different monetary policy environments. The federal funds target displays clear changes over time rather than a uniform distribution, and several predictors appear to move in related patterns. The correlation analysis also suggests that some variables are highly related, which supports paying attention to multicollinearity and model flexibility in the later modeling stage.

# Research Question 1

This section studies how the federal funds target is related to selected macroeconomic and financial variables, and whether those relationships remain stable over time.

## Variable Selection

```{r}
data_rq2 <- df_final %>%
  arrange(date)

vars <- c(
  "ff_target",
  "core_pce_yoy", "inflation_gap",
  "UNRATE", "payems_yoy",
  "term_spread_10y_3m", "BAA10Y", "ANFCI",
  "fomc_meetings", "days_since_last_fomc"
)

df_full_rq2 <- data_rq2[, vars]
na_ratio <- colMeans(is.na(df_full_rq2))
df_clean_rq2 <- df_full_rq2[, na_ratio < 0.2]
```

```{r}
x <- model.matrix(ff_target ~ ., df_clean_rq2)[, -1]
y <- df_clean_rq2$ff_target

lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)

coef(lasso, s = "lambda.min")
```

Variable selection narrows the model to a smaller set of predictors that appear most relevant to the policy rate.

## Final Regression Dataset

```{r}
df_reg_rq2 <- data_rq2[, c(
  "date", "ff_target", "core_pce_yoy", "UNRATE",
  "term_spread_10y_3m", "BAA10Y", "ANFCI"
)]
```

The regression section uses a focused set of explanatory variables rather than the full macro dataset.

## Exploratory Time-Series Checks

```{r}
plot(df_reg_rq2$date, df_reg_rq2$ff_target, type = "l", main = "Federal Funds Target Rate")

plot(df_reg_rq2$date, df_reg_rq2$core_pce_yoy, type = "l", main = "Core PCE Inflation (YoY %)")

plot(df_reg_rq2$date, df_reg_rq2$UNRATE, type = "l", main = "Unemployment Rate")

plot(df_reg_rq2$date, df_reg_rq2$term_spread_10y_3m, type = "l", main = "Term Spread")

cor(df_reg_rq2[, -1], use = "complete.obs")
```

These plots and the correlation matrix give a first look at the time-series behavior and cross-variable relationships before formal estimation.

## ADF Tests

```{r}
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$ff_target)
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$core_pce_yoy)
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$UNRATE)
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$term_spread_10y_3m)
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$BAA10Y)
adf.test(df_reg_rq2$ANFCI)
```

The ADF tests motivate the later robustness checks in differences and the stability analysis.

## Baseline Model

```{r}
model_baseline <- lm(
  ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE + term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
  data = df_reg_rq2
)

summary(model_baseline)
```

The baseline model estimates the full-sample association between the policy rate and the selected explanatory variables.

## Robustness Check 1: Dynamic Model

```{r}
df_reg_rq2$ff_target_lag1 <- dplyr::lag(df_reg_rq2$ff_target, 1)

model_dyn <- lm(
  ff_target ~ ff_target_lag1 + core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
    term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
  data = df_reg_rq2
)

summary(model_dyn)
```

The dynamic specification captures persistence in the policy rate through a lagged dependent variable.

## Robustness Check 2: Differenced Model

```{r}
df_diff <- data.frame(
  date = df_reg_rq2$date[-1],
  d_ff = diff(df_reg_rq2$ff_target),
  d_core_pce = diff(df_reg_rq2$core_pce_yoy),
  d_unrate = diff(df_reg_rq2$UNRATE),
  term_spread_10y_3m = df_reg_rq2$term_spread_10y_3m[-1]
)

model_diff <- lm(
  d_ff ~ d_core_pce + d_unrate + term_spread_10y_3m,
  data = df_diff
)

summary(model_diff)
```

The first-difference model checks whether the main relationships remain visible when the focus shifts from levels to short-run changes.

## Rolling Coefficient Plots

```{r}
get_coef <- function(idx) {
  window_data <- df_reg_rq2[idx, ]
  coef(lm(
    ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
      term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
    data = window_data
  ))
}

roll <- rollapply(
  data = 1:nrow(df_reg_rq2),
  width = 60,
  FUN = get_coef,
  by = 1,
  align = "right"
)

roll <- as.data.frame(roll)
roll_dates <- df_reg_rq2$date[60:nrow(df_reg_rq2)]
```

```{r}
plot(roll_dates, roll$core_pce_yoy, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: core_pce_yoy",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")

plot(roll_dates, roll$UNRATE, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: UNRATE",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")

plot(roll_dates, roll$term_spread_10y_3m, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: Term Spread",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")
```

Rolling coefficients provide a visual way to assess whether the reaction function changes across different periods.

## Breakpoint Analysis

```{r}
rq1_formula <- ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
  term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI

bp <- breakpoints(rq1_formula, data = df_reg_rq2, breaks = BP_MAX_BREAKS)

summary(bp)
plot(bp)
```

```{r}
# Number of breaks is a setting (BP_N_BREAKS); the dates come from the fitted
# model. BIC's own choice is printed for comparison.
bic_breaks <- length(breakpoints(bp)$breakpoints)
bic_breaks

bp_rows  <- breakpoints(bp, breaks = BP_N_BREAKS)$breakpoints
n_breaks <- length(bp_rows)
bp_dates <- df_reg_rq2$date[bp_rows]

n_breaks
bp_dates
confint(bp, breaks = n_breaks)
```

```{r}
plot(df_reg_rq2$date, df_reg_rq2$ff_target, type = "l")
abline(v = bp_dates, col = "red")
```

The analysis uses `r n_breaks` breaks, estimated at `r paste(format(bp_dates, "%b %Y"), collapse = ", ")`. BIC alone would pick `r bic_breaks`, the most the test allows; with trending variables and serially correlated errors BIC tends to over-select breaks, so the number of breaks is kept as an explicit choice.

## Chow Tests

```{r}
chow_dates <- sort(unique(c(CHOW_EVENT_DATES, bp_dates)))

for (d in as.list(chow_dates)) {
  idx <- which(df_reg_rq2$date == d)
  if (length(idx) > 0) {
    test <- sctest(rq1_formula, type = "Chow", point = idx, data = df_reg_rq2)
    cat("Date:", format(d),
        if (d %in% bp_dates) "(estimated break)" else "(event)",
        "| F =", round(test$statistic, 2),
        "| p-value =", format(test$p.value, scientific = TRUE), "\n")
  }
}
```

The Chow tests evaluate whether the regression relationship shifts at both estimated and theory-motivated break dates.

## Sub-Period Regressions

```{r}
# Sub-periods run between the estimated break dates.
period_starts <- c(min(df_reg_rq2$date), bp_dates)
period_ends   <- c(bp_dates, max(df_reg_rq2$date) + 1)
period_labels <- paste0(format(period_starts, "%Y"), "-", format(period_ends - 1, "%Y"))

df_reg_rq2$period <- cut(
  df_reg_rq2$date,
  breaks = c(period_starts, max(df_reg_rq2$date) + 1),
  labels = period_labels,
  right = FALSE
)

models <- lapply(period_labels, function(p) {
  lm(rq1_formula, data = subset(df_reg_rq2, period == p))
})
names(models) <- period_labels

lapply(models, summary)
```

```{r}
coef_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(models, coef))
coef_table
```

```{r}
coef_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(p) {
  df <- tidy(models[[p]])
  df$period <- p
  return(df)
}))

coef_table
```

```{r}
ggplot(coef_table[coef_table$term != "(Intercept)", ],
       aes(x = period, y = estimate, color = term, group = term)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

Sub-period regressions make it easier to interpret how the policy rule differs across historical regimes.

# Research Question 2

## Data Preparation

```{r}
data_rq1 <- df_final %>%
  arrange(date)

data_rq1$policy_change <- as.numeric(data_rq1$policy_change)
```

The dataset is sorted in chronological order so the clustering results can later be interpreted as evolving regimes rather than disconnected groups.

## Event-Sensitive Feature Construction

```{r}
data_rq1$ff_change_1m     <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$ff_target))
data_rq1$unrate_change_1m <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$UNRATE))
data_rq1$oil_change_1m    <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$WTISPLC))
data_rq1$house_change_1m  <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$HOUST))
data_rq1$credit_change_1m <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$BAA10Y))
data_rq1$fci_change_1m    <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$ANFCI))
data_rq1$infl_change_1m   <- c(NA, diff(data_rq1$core_pce_yoy))
```

Monthly changes were added so the clustering can reflect both the level of macroeconomic conditions and how quickly those conditions are shifting.

## Missingness Screening

```{r}
num_data <- data_rq1[, setdiff(names(data_rq1), "date")]
num_data <- num_data[, sapply(num_data, is.numeric)]

na_share <- colMeans(is.na(num_data))
na_share
```

```{r}
num_data <- num_data[, na_share <= 0.20]
```

Variables with more than 20% missingness were excluded from the initial numeric screening step to keep the clustering input reasonably complete.

## Variable Selection for Clustering

```{r}
cluster_vars_model <- c(
  "ff_target",
  "PCEPILFE",
  "MICH",
  "UNRATE",
  "HOUST",
  "T10Y3M",
  "BAA10Y",
  "ANFCI",
  "WTISPLC",
  "core_pce_yoy",
  "payems_yoy",
  "ff_change_1m",
  "unrate_change_1m",
  "oil_change_1m",
  "credit_change_1m",
  "fci_change_1m",
  "infl_change_1m"
)

cluster_vars_extra <- c(
  "policy_change",
  "fomc_meetings",
  "fomc_scheduled",
  "fomc_unscheduled",
  "days_since_last_fomc"
)

cluster_vars_model <- intersect(cluster_vars_model, names(data_rq1))
cluster_vars_extra <- intersect(cluster_vars_extra, names(data_rq1))

cluster_df <- data_rq1[, c("date", cluster_vars_model, cluster_vars_extra)]
cluster_df <- na.omit(cluster_df)

cluster_x <- cluster_df[, cluster_vars_model]
cluster_x_extra <- cluster_df[, cluster_vars_extra]
dates <- cluster_df$date

nrow(cluster_x)
```

The model variables are used for clustering itself, while the extra variables are kept for later interpretation of the resulting regimes.

## Correlation Check on Final Clustering Inputs

```{r}
cor_mat2 <- cor(cluster_x)
corrplot(cor_mat2, method = "color", tl.cex = 0.6)
```

```{r}
remove_auto <- findCorrelation(cor_mat2, cutoff = 0.9, names = TRUE)
cat("Variables removed due to high correlation:\n")
print(remove_auto)

cluster_x2 <- cluster_x[, !names(cluster_x) %in% remove_auto]
```

## Scaling and PCA

```{r}
cluster_scaled <- scale(cluster_x2)

pca <- prcomp(cluster_scaled)
summary(pca)
```

```{r}
plot(pca, type = "l", main = "Scree Plot")
```

```{r}
cum_var <- cumsum(pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2))
cum_var
```

```{r}
n_pc <- which(cum_var >= 0.80)[1]
cat("Number of PCs explaining at least 80% variance:", n_pc, "\n")

pc_scores <- pca$x[, 1:n_pc, drop = FALSE]
head(pc_scores)
```

PCA is used to reduce dimensionality while retaining most of the variation in the clustering inputs.

## Clustering

```{r}
fviz_nbclust(pc_scores, kmeans, method = "wss")
fviz_nbclust(pc_scores, kmeans, method = "silhouette")
```

```{r}
# Silhouette diagnostics over K_RANGE; k itself is a setting (K_CLUSTERS).
set.seed(123)
dist_pc <- dist(pc_scores)
avg_sil <- sapply(K_RANGE, function(kk) {
  fit <- kmeans(pc_scores, centers = kk, nstart = 50)
  mean(silhouette(fit$cluster, dist_pc)[, "sil_width"])
})
data.frame(k = K_RANGE, avg_silhouette = round(avg_sil, 3))

k <- K_CLUSTERS
set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(pc_scores, centers = k, nstart = 100)

result <- data.frame(
  date = dates,
  cluster = factor(km$cluster),
  cluster_x_extra
)

head(result)
```

The clustering uses k-means on the retained principal components. The analysis uses k = `r k` clusters. Average silhouette widths for k = `r min(K_RANGE)` to `r max(K_RANGE)` are all between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(avg_sil))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(avg_sil))`, which indicates weak cluster structure, so k is kept as an explicit choice rather than picked by silhouette.

# Research Question 3

This section turns the meeting-level data into a multiclass classification problem and compares tuned machine-learning models against a naive benchmark.

## Data Preparation

```{r}
df_rq3 <- df_final %>%
  arrange(date)

df_rq3$policy_change <- as.integer(df_rq3$policy_change)
```

The data are restructured at the FOMC meeting level so the prediction task matches actual decision points.


## Meeting-Level Target

Each row is one **scheduled** FOMC meeting, labelled by what was decided at that meeting.

**Label rule.** The label compares the target the day before the meeting starts with the target `r LABEL_WINDOW_DAYS` days after the decision. Rate changes often take effect the day after the announcement, so the window has to extend past the decision date. Since 1986, 124 of 150 target changes fall inside such a window. The other 26 were intermeeting moves made by the Chair between meetings (all in 1986–1992). They are not decisions of any meeting, so they are not attributed to one.

**Why scheduled meetings only.** Conference calls and unscheduled meetings are excluded:

- They respond to sudden shocks (9/11, January and October 2008, COVID). The predictors are last month's macro data, which cannot see those shocks coming, so every model misses them for the same reason. They add noise to the comparison, not information about the models.
- Whether an emergency call happens at all is itself a signal of stress. Mixing those rows with regular meetings changes what is being predicted.
- Scheduled meetings happen on known dates (about eight a year), so every row is a decision the Fed was going to make regardless. That matches the question: how do model families compare at predicting the decision at each meeting.

Emergency moves are not discarded from the data. They remain in the target series and could be used as a predictor later ("was there an intermeeting move since the last meeting?").

The previous version of this section labelled meetings from the change in the *monthly average* target between meeting months. A move late in one month raised the next month's average, so later holds were labelled as hikes or cuts. Two meetings in the same month were also merged into one row.

```{r}
target_daily <- read.csv("data/fed_target_daily.csv") %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>%
  arrange(date)

# Target in effect on a given day (last observation on or before it).
target_asof <- function(d) {
  target_daily$ff_target[findInterval(as.numeric(d), as.numeric(target_daily$date))]
}

meetings_rq3 <- read.csv("data/fomc_meetings.csv") %>%
  filter(type == "scheduled") %>%
  mutate(
    start_date    = as.Date(start_date),
    decision_date = as.Date(decision_date),
    month         = as.Date(format(start_date, "%Y-%m-01"))
  ) %>%
  filter(month >= SAMPLE_START, month <= SAMPLE_END) %>%
  mutate(
    target_before = target_asof(start_date - 1),
    target_after  = target_asof(decision_date + LABEL_WINDOW_DAYS),
    target_change = target_after - target_before,
    policy_action_class = factor(
      case_when(
        target_change > 0 ~ "hike",
        target_change < 0 ~ "cut",
        TRUE              ~ "hold"
      ),
      levels = c("cut", "hold", "hike")
    )
  )

meetings_rq3 %>%
  count(policy_action_class) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))
```

## Lagged Predictors

```{r}
exclude_from_lag <- c(
  "date",
  "ff_target",
  "unrate_lag1",
  "term_spread_10y_3m"
)

df_rq3_lagged <- df_rq3 %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      -all_of(exclude_from_lag),
      ~ lag(.x),
      .names = "{.col}_lag1"
    )
  )

# Each meeting gets the previous month's values (the `_lag1` columns of the
# month the meeting starts in). `date` becomes the decision date.
df_meeting_model <- meetings_rq3 %>%
  select(month, decision_date, policy_action_class) %>%
  left_join(
    df_rq3_lagged %>% select(date, ends_with("_lag1")),
    by = c("month" = "date")
  ) %>%
  rename(date = decision_date) %>%
  select(-month) %>%
  arrange(date)

df_meeting_model %>%
  count(policy_action_class) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))
```

Only lagged information is used so that the predictors reflect information available before the meeting.

## Complete Predictor Set

```{r}
lagged_predictors <- names(df_meeting_model)[grepl("_lag1$", names(df_meeting_model))]

lagged_predictors_complete <- lagged_predictors[
  sapply(df_meeting_model[, lagged_predictors], function(x) sum(is.na(x)) == 0)
]

df_final_rq3 <- df_meeting_model %>%
  select(date, policy_action_class, all_of(lagged_predictors_complete)) %>%
  select(
    -core_pce_yoy_lag1,
    -PCEPI_lag1,
    -DGS3MO_lag1,
    -PAYEMS_lag1,
    -DGS10_lag1
  )

str(df_final_rq3)
table(df_final_rq3$policy_action_class)
```

This step keeps only complete lagged predictors and removes a few highly redundant variables.

## Train/Test Split

```{r}
df_final_rq3$policy_action_class <- factor(
  df_final_rq3$policy_action_class,
  levels = c("cut", "hold", "hike")
)

n <- nrow(df_final_rq3)
train_size <- floor(0.8 * n)

train_data <- df_final_rq3[1:train_size, ]
test_data  <- df_final_rq3[(train_size + 1):n, ]

train_data$policy_action_class <- factor(
  train_data$policy_action_class,
  levels = c("cut", "hold", "hike")
)

test_data$policy_action_class <- factor(
  test_data$policy_action_class,
  levels = c("cut", "hold", "hike")
)

prop.table(table(train_data$policy_action_class))
prop.table(table(test_data$policy_action_class))
```

A chronological split is used so the evaluation respects time order.

## Metric Helpers

```{r}
get_metrics <- function(pred, truth) {
  cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, truth)

  by_class <- as.data.frame(cm$byClass)

  precision <- by_class[, "Pos Pred Value"]
  recall <- by_class[, "Sensitivity"]
  bal_acc <- by_class[, "Balanced Accuracy"]

  f1 <- ifelse(
    (precision + recall) == 0,
    NA,
    2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  )

  list(
    cm = cm,
    summary = data.frame(
      Macro_F1 = mean(f1, na.rm = TRUE),
      Mean_Balanced_Accuracy = mean(bal_acc, na.rm = TRUE),
      Kappa = unname(cm$overall["Kappa"]),
      Accuracy = unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"])
    )
  )
}

rank_metric_table <- function(results_df) {
  results_df %>%
    arrange(
      desc(Macro_F1),
      desc(Mean_Balanced_Accuracy),
      desc(Kappa),
      desc(Accuracy)
    )
}
```

`get_metrics()` is what the tuning functions use to compare settings on the
inner validation block.

### Scoring rule for the comparison

Models are compared on **macro-F1**: the F1 score for each class (cut, hold,
hike), averaged with equal weight. A model that never predicts a class gets
F1 = 0 for that class. An earlier version dropped such classes from the
average, which scored "always hold" on the hold class alone and ranked it
first; it never catches a move, so it should not. A class's F1 is left out
only when it appears neither in the predictions nor in the actual outcomes.

Ties are broken by **balanced accuracy** (the average of the three class
recalls). Kappa and accuracy are reported too. Accuracy alone rewards
predicting hold, since about 70% of meetings are holds.

```{r}
RQ3_CLASSES <- c("cut", "hold", "hike")

class_scores <- function(pred, truth) {
  tab <- table(
    Predicted = factor(pred, levels = RQ3_CLASSES),
    Actual    = factor(truth, levels = RQ3_CLASSES)
  )
  tp <- diag(tab)
  fp <- rowSums(tab) - tp
  fn <- colSums(tab) - tp
  tibble(
    Class     = RQ3_CLASSES,
    Actual    = as.integer(colSums(tab)),
    Predicted = as.integer(rowSums(tab)),
    Precision = ifelse(tp + fp == 0, 0, tp / (tp + fp)),
    Recall    = ifelse(tp + fn == 0, NA, tp / (tp + fn)),
    F1        = ifelse(2 * tp + fp + fn == 0, NA, 2 * tp / (2 * tp + fp + fn))
  )
}

macro_f1 <- function(pred, truth) mean(class_scores(pred, truth)$F1, na.rm = TRUE)

cohen_kappa <- function(pred, truth) {
  tab <- table(factor(pred, levels = RQ3_CLASSES), factor(truth, levels = RQ3_CLASSES))
  n  <- sum(tab)
  po <- sum(diag(tab)) / n
  pe <- sum(rowSums(tab) * colSums(tab)) / n^2
  if (pe == 1) return(0)
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}

score_predictions <- function(pred, truth) {
  cs <- class_scores(pred, truth)
  tibble(
    Macro_F1          = mean(cs$F1, na.rm = TRUE),
    Balanced_Accuracy = mean(cs$Recall, na.rm = TRUE),
    Kappa             = cohen_kappa(pred, truth),
    Accuracy          = mean(as.character(pred) == as.character(truth)),
    n                 = length(truth)
  )
}

rank_scores <- function(scores) {
  scores %>% arrange(desc(Macro_F1), desc(Balanced_Accuracy), desc(Kappa), desc(Accuracy))
}
```

## Inner Validation Helpers

```{r}
make_inner_split <- function(train_part, valid_frac = 0.2) {
  n <- nrow(train_part)
  valid_size <- max(10, floor(valid_frac * n))

  inner_train <- train_part[1:(n - valid_size), ]
  inner_valid <- train_part[(n - valid_size + 1):n, ]

  list(
    inner_train = inner_train,
    inner_valid = inner_valid
  )
}

to_xgb_label <- function(y_factor) {
  as.integer(y_factor) - 1
}
```

The inner split is also chronological so tuning remains time-aware.

## Tuned Models

```{r}
tune_multinom <- function(train_part) {
  split_obj <- make_inner_split(train_part)
  inner_train <- split_obj$inner_train
  inner_valid <- split_obj$inner_valid

  decay_grid <- c(0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1)
  results <- list()

  for (d in decay_grid) {
    fit <- multinom(
      policy_action_class ~ . - date,
      data = inner_train,
      decay = d,
      trace = FALSE,
      MaxNWts = 5000
    )

    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = inner_valid)
    metric_row <- get_metrics(pred, inner_valid$policy_action_class)$summary

    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- cbind(
      data.frame(decay = d),
      metric_row
    )
  }

  results_df <- bind_rows(results) %>%
    rank_metric_table()

  best_decay <- results_df$decay[1]

  final_fit <- multinom(
    policy_action_class ~ . - date,
    data = train_part,
    decay = best_decay,
    trace = FALSE,
    MaxNWts = 5000
  )

  list(
    best_params = results_df[1, ],
    tuning_results = results_df,
    final_fit = final_fit
  )
}
```

```{r}
tune_enet <- function(train_part) {
  split_obj <- make_inner_split(train_part)
  inner_train <- split_obj$inner_train
  inner_valid <- split_obj$inner_valid

  x_inner_train <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = inner_train)[, -1]
  y_inner_train <- inner_train$policy_action_class

  x_inner_valid <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = inner_valid)[, -1]
  y_inner_valid <- inner_valid$policy_action_class

  alpha_grid <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
  results <- list()

  for (a in alpha_grid) {
    cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(
      x = x_inner_train,
      y = y_inner_train,
      family = "multinomial",
      alpha = a,
      type.measure = "class",
      nfolds = 5,
      standardize = TRUE,
      nlambda = 50,
      lambda.min.ratio = 1e-3,
      maxit = 200000
    )

    pred <- predict(
      cv_fit,
      newx = x_inner_valid,
      s = "lambda.1se",
      type = "class"
    )

    pred <- factor(as.vector(pred), levels = levels(y_inner_valid))
    metric_row <- get_metrics(pred, y_inner_valid)$summary

    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- cbind(
      data.frame(alpha = a, lambda = cv_fit$lambda.1se),
      metric_row
    )
  }

  results_df <- bind_rows(results) %>%
    rank_metric_table()

  best_alpha <- results_df$alpha[1]

  x_train <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = train_part)[, -1]
  y_train <- train_part$policy_action_class

  final_fit <- cv.glmnet(
    x = x_train,
    y = y_train,
    family = "multinomial",
    alpha = best_alpha,
    type.measure = "class",
    nfolds = 5,
    standardize = TRUE,
    nlambda = 50,
    maxit = 200000
  )

  list(
    best_params = results_df[1, ],
    tuning_results = results_df,
    final_fit = final_fit
  )
}
```

```{r}
tune_rf <- function(train_part) {
  split_obj <- make_inner_split(train_part)
  inner_train <- split_obj$inner_train
  inner_valid <- split_obj$inner_valid

  p <- ncol(inner_train %>% select(-date, -policy_action_class))

  mtry_grid <- unique(pmax(1, c(floor(sqrt(p)), floor(p / 3), floor(p / 2))))
  nodesize_grid <- c(1, 3, 5)
  ntree_grid <- c(300, 500, 1000)

  results <- list()

  for (m in mtry_grid) {
    for (ns in nodesize_grid) {
      for (nt in ntree_grid) {
        fit <- randomForest(
          policy_action_class ~ . - date,
          data = inner_train,
          ntree = nt,
          mtry = m,
          nodesize = ns,
          importance = TRUE
        )

        pred <- predict(fit, newdata = inner_valid)
        metric_row <- get_metrics(pred, inner_valid$policy_action_class)$summary

        results[[length(results) + 1]] <- cbind(
          data.frame(mtry = m, nodesize = ns, ntree = nt),
          metric_row
        )
      }
    }
  }

  results_df <- bind_rows(results) %>%
    rank_metric_table()

  best_mtry <- results_df$mtry[1]
  best_nodesize <- results_df$nodesize[1]
  best_ntree <- results_df$ntree[1]

  final_fit <- randomForest(
    policy_action_class ~ . - date,
    data = train_part,
    ntree = best_ntree,
    mtry = best_mtry,
    nodesize = best_nodesize,
    importance = TRUE
  )

  list(
    best_params = results_df[1, ],
    tuning_results = results_df,
    final_fit = final_fit
  )
}
```

```{r}
tune_xgb <- function(train_part) {
  split_obj <- make_inner_split(train_part)
  inner_train <- split_obj$inner_train
  inner_valid <- split_obj$inner_valid

  x_inner_train <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = inner_train)[, -1]
  y_inner_train <- to_xgb_label(inner_train$policy_action_class)

  x_inner_valid <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = inner_valid)[, -1]
  y_inner_valid_factor <- inner_valid$policy_action_class

  dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_inner_train, label = y_inner_train)
  dvalid <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_inner_valid)

  eta_grid <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1)
  max_depth_grid <- c(1, 2, 3)
  nrounds_grid <- c(100, 300, 500)
  min_child_weight_grid <- c(1, 3)

  results <- list()

  for (eta_val in eta_grid) {
    for (depth_val in max_depth_grid) {
      for (nrounds_val in nrounds_grid) {
        for (mcw_val in min_child_weight_grid) {

          fit <- xgb.train(
            params = list(
              objective = "multi:softmax",
              num_class = 3,
              eval_metric = "merror",
              eta = eta_val,
              max_depth = depth_val,
              min_child_weight = mcw_val,
              subsample = 1,
              colsample_bytree = 1
            ),
            data = dtrain,
            nrounds = nrounds_val,
            verbose = 0
          )

          pred_numeric <- predict(fit, newdata = dvalid)
          pred_factor <- factor(
            c("cut", "hold", "hike")[pred_numeric + 1],
            levels = c("cut", "hold", "hike")
          )

          metric_row <- get_metrics(pred_factor, y_inner_valid_factor)$summary

          results[[length(results) + 1]] <- cbind(
            data.frame(
              eta = eta_val,
              max_depth = depth_val,
              nrounds = nrounds_val,
              min_child_weight = mcw_val
            ),
            metric_row
          )
        }
      }
    }
  }

  results_df <- bind_rows(results) %>%
    rank_metric_table()

  best <- results_df[1, ]

  x_train <- model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = train_part)[, -1]
  y_train <- to_xgb_label(train_part$policy_action_class)

  dtrain_full <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_train, label = y_train)

  final_fit <- xgb.train(
    params = list(
      objective = "multi:softmax",
      num_class = 3,
      eval_metric = "merror",
      eta = best$eta,
      max_depth = best$max_depth,
      min_child_weight = best$min_child_weight,
      subsample = 1,
      colsample_bytree = 1
    ),
    data = dtrain_full,
    nrounds = best$nrounds,
    verbose = 0
  )

  list(
    best_params = best,
    tuning_results = results_df,
    final_fit = final_fit
  )
}
```

These tuning functions keep the model-fitting section organized while preserving the full comparison pipeline.

## Model Registry

Every model, including the baseline, is a pair of functions: `tune()` fits
it on a training window (with time-ordered inner validation) and
`predict()` returns cut / hold / hike for new meetings. The held-out split
and the expanding-window evaluation both run through `fit_and_predict()`,
so every model is evaluated by identical code.

The baseline always predicts hold and acts as a naive benchmark.

```{r rq3-registry}
as_class <- function(x) factor(as.vector(x), levels = RQ3_CLASSES)
rq3_x <- function(data) model.matrix(policy_action_class ~ . - date, data = data)[, -1]

rq3_models <- list(
  Baseline_Hold = list(
    tune    = function(train_part) list(best_params = NULL),
    predict = function(obj, newdata) as_class(rep("hold", nrow(newdata)))
  ),
  Multinomial_Logit_Tuned = list(
    tune    = tune_multinom,
    predict = function(obj, newdata) as_class(predict(obj$final_fit, newdata = newdata))
  ),
  Elastic_Net_Tuned = list(
    tune    = tune_enet,
    predict = function(obj, newdata) {
      as_class(predict(obj$final_fit, newx = rq3_x(newdata), s = "lambda.1se", type = "class"))
    }
  ),
  Random_Forest_Tuned = list(
    tune    = tune_rf,
    predict = function(obj, newdata) as_class(predict(obj$final_fit, newdata = newdata))
  ),
  XGBoost_Tuned = list(
    tune    = tune_xgb,
    predict = function(obj, newdata) {
      as_class(RQ3_CLASSES[predict(obj$final_fit, newdata = xgb.DMatrix(data = rq3_x(newdata))) + 1])
    }
  )
)

fit_and_predict <- function(train_part, test_part, models = rq3_models) {
  map(models, function(m) {
    obj <- m$tune(train_part)
    list(obj = obj, pred = m$predict(obj, test_part))
  })
}
```

## Held-Out Test Evaluation

```{r rq3-inputs-hash}
# Fingerprint of everything the two cached RQ3 chunks depend on: data,
# settings, tuning/metric functions and package versions. If any of these
# change, knitr re-runs the cached chunks; otherwise it reuses the results.
fn_code <- function(...) lapply(list(...), deparse)
rq3_inputs_hash <- digest::digest(list(
  df_final_rq3, train_data, test_data, RQ3_START_TRAIN, RQ3_STEP,
  fn_code(tune_multinom, tune_enet, tune_rf, tune_xgb, get_metrics,
          make_inner_split, to_xgb_label, rank_metric_table, fit_and_predict,
          as_class, rq3_x),
  lapply(rq3_models, function(m) lapply(m, deparse)),
  lapply(sessionInfo()$otherPkgs, `[[`, "Version")
))
```

```{r rq3-holdout, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=rq3_inputs_hash}
holdout <- fit_and_predict(train_data, test_data)
```

This block tunes each model on the first 80% of meetings and predicts the
last 20% once. One split is a single period with few moves, so it is not
used to rank the models (the expanding-window evaluation below is). It is
kept for the confusion matrices, tuned settings and variable importance.

## Held-Out Results

```{r}
holdout_scores <- imap_dfr(holdout, ~ score_predictions(.x$pred, test_data$policy_action_class) %>%
  mutate(Model = .y, .before = 1)) %>%
  rank_scores()

holdout_scores
```

```{r}
map(holdout, ~ table(Predicted = .x$pred, Actual = test_data$policy_action_class))
```

```{r}
map(holdout[-1], ~ .x$obj$best_params)
```

```{r}
rf_importance <- importance(rf_fit)

rf_importance_df <- data.frame(

  MeanDecreaseAccuracy = rf_importance[, "MeanDecreaseAccuracy"],
  MeanDecreaseGini = rf_importance[, "MeanDecreaseGini"]
) %>%

head(rf_importance_df, 10)
```

```{r}
xgb_fit <- holdout$XGBoost_Tuned$obj$final_fit
xgb_feature_names <- colnames(rq3_x(train_data))

xgb_importance <- xgb.importance(
  feature_names = xgb_feature_names,
  model = xgb_fit
)

head(xgb_importance, 10)
```

Variable importance helps interpret which lagged macro variables are most useful for predicting meeting outcomes.

## Expanding-Window Evaluation (Main Comparison)

The models are ranked here. The first training window holds the first
`r RQ3_START_TRAIN` meetings. Each fold tunes every model on all meetings
so far and predicts the next `r RQ3_STEP`; then the window grows and the
next block is predicted. Every meeting after the first window is predicted
exactly once, by models that saw only earlier meetings.

```{r rq3-rolling, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=rq3_inputs_hash}
n_meetings <- nrow(df_final_rq3)
fold_ends  <- seq(RQ3_START_TRAIN, n_meetings - 1, by = RQ3_STEP)

# Each fold: tune every model on meetings 1..end_train, predict the next
# RQ3_STEP meetings (fewer in the last fold). Keep every out-of-sample
# prediction so all scores are computed afterwards from one table.
rolling <- map(seq_along(fold_ends), function(fold) {
  end_train  <- fold_ends[fold]
  train_part <- df_final_rq3[1:end_train, ]
  test_part  <- df_final_rq3[(end_train + 1):min(end_train + RQ3_STEP, n_meetings), ]

  fits <- fit_and_predict(train_part, test_part)

  list(
    info = data.frame(
      Fold = fold,
      Train_End  = max(train_part$date),
      Test_Start = min(test_part$date),
      Test_End   = max(test_part$date)
    ),
    preds = imap_dfr(fits, ~ tibble(
      Fold  = fold,
      Model = .y,
      date  = test_part$date,
      truth = test_part$policy_action_class,
      pred  = .x$pred
    )),
    tuning = imap(fits[-1], ~ cbind(Fold = fold, Model = .y, .x$obj$best_params))
  )
})

fold_info     <- map_dfr(rolling, "info")
rolling_preds <- map_dfr(rolling, "preds")
tuning_table  <- bind_rows(flatten(map(rolling, "tuning")))
```

### Pooled Scores

Each test block holds only `r RQ3_STEP` meetings, and many blocks contain no
cut or no hike, so a score computed per block is noisy and often undefined.
Instead, the out-of-sample predictions from all
`r nrow(fold_info)` folds (`r n_distinct(rolling_preds$date)` meetings,
`r format(min(rolling_preds$date), "%b %Y")` to
`r format(max(rolling_preds$date), "%b %Y")`) are pooled and each model is
scored once.

```{r}
rolling_scores <- rolling_preds %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  group_modify(~ score_predictions(.x$pred, .x$truth)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rank_scores()

rolling_scores
```

### How Sure Is the Ranking?

With about `r n_distinct(rolling_preds$date)` test meetings, small gaps
between models can be luck. A moving-block bootstrap resamples blocks of
`r RQ3_BOOT_BLOCK` consecutive meetings (keeping runs of hikes or cuts
together) `r RQ3_BOOT_REPS` times and re-scores every model on the same
resample. The table gives a 90% interval for each model's macro-F1 and for
its gap to the best baseline. An interval for the gap that includes zero
means the data cannot tell the model apart from that baseline.

```{r}
block_bootstrap_f1 <- function(preds, reps, block, seed) {
  dates <- sort(unique(preds$date))
  n <- length(dates)
  wide <- preds %>%
    select(Model, date, truth, pred) %>%
    arrange(date)
  by_model <- split(wide, wide$Model)

  set.seed(seed)
  map_dfr(seq_len(reps), function(r) {
    starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
    idx <- unlist(lapply(starts, function(s) s:(s + block - 1)))[1:n]
    imap_dfr(by_model, ~ tibble(rep = r, Model = .y,
                                Macro_F1 = macro_f1(.x$pred[idx], .x$truth[idx])))
  })
}

boot_f1 <- block_bootstrap_f1(rolling_preds, RQ3_BOOT_REPS, RQ3_BOOT_BLOCK, RQ3_SEED)

best_baseline <- rolling_scores %>%
  filter(startsWith(Model, "Baseline_")) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  pull(Model)

rolling_intervals <- boot_f1 %>%
  group_by(rep) %>%
  mutate(Gap = Macro_F1 - Macro_F1[Model == best_baseline]) %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  summarise(
    F1_low  = quantile(Macro_F1, 0.05),
    F1_high = quantile(Macro_F1, 0.95),
    Gap_low  = quantile(Gap, 0.05),
    Gap_high = quantile(Gap, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rolling_ranking <- rolling_scores %>%
  select(Model, Macro_F1, Balanced_Accuracy, Kappa, Accuracy) %>%
  left_join(rolling_intervals, by = "Model")

rolling_ranking
```

Best baseline: `r best_baseline`.

```{r}
ggplot(rolling_ranking, aes(x = reorder(Model, Macro_F1), y = Macro_F1)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = F1_low, ymax = F1_high)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Expanding-window macro-F1 by model (90% block-bootstrap interval)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Macro-F1 (pooled out-of-sample predictions)"
  )
```

### Class-wise Results

```{r}
rolling_class_scores <- rolling_preds %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  group_modify(~ class_scores(.x$pred, .x$truth)) %>%
  ungroup()

rolling_class_scores
```

This shows which moves each model catches: recall is the share of actual
cuts (or hikes, or holds) the model predicted correctly.

### Stability Across Folds

```{r}
fold_scores <- rolling_preds %>%
  group_by(Fold, Model) %>%
  group_modify(~ score_predictions(.x$pred, .x$truth)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(fold_info, by = "Fold")

ggplot(fold_scores, aes(x = Test_Start, y = Macro_F1, color = Model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Macro-F1 per test block",
    x = "Start of test block",
    y = "Macro-F1"
  )
```

Per-block scores swing widely because each block has few moves; they show
when models do well or badly, not which model is better overall.
